answer.label: Not Henry David Thoreau — actually Henry Stanley Haskins
answer.authorDates: 1875–1957 · Wall Street trader and anonymous aphorist
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from Meditations in Wall Street (New York: William Morrow & Co., 1940), page 131 — a book of aphorisms published anonymously with an introduction by Albert Jay Nock. Quote Investigator ↗ gives that 1940 printing as the earliest appearance it located and credits the Wall Street trader Henry Stanley Haskins, whom The New York Times named as the anonymous author in 1947.

source.excerpt: What lies behind us and what lies before us are tiny matters compared to what lies within us.
trail: 1940 — Meditations in Wall Street is published by William Morrow & Company with no author named and an introduction by Albert Jay Nock; Wikipedia’s entry on Nock lists the book in his bibliography as “Meditations in Wall Street, with an introduction by Albert Jay Nock. W. Morrow & Company, 1940” ↗. The sentence stands on page 131.

1947 — The New York Times identifies the anonymous author as Henry S. Haskins, according to Quote Investigator’s citation list ↗, which also records a 1974 Forbes item crediting the publisher’s name instead.

1980, then 1989 — the line is credited to Ralph Waldo Emerson, and later to Oliver Wendell Holmes in a self-help bestseller; Wikiquote now carries it in the Misattributed section of Emerson’s page ↗, pointing back to Haskins.

1990s onward — Thoreau’s name is attached in spiritual-guidance books, which is why the Walden Woods Project’s Mis-Quotation Page ↗ lists it with the correction: Henry Stanley Haskins (1875–1957), Meditations in Wall Street, p. 131.
source.excerptNote: Three wordings circulate. Quote Investigator transcribes page 131 of the 1940 book with “what lies before us”; the widely repeated popular form, printed by both the Walden Woods Project and Wikiquote when they correct the attribution, reads “what lies ahead of us.” The Thoreau credit rides a third, extended variant — “small matters” plus a closing line about miracles happening — which Quote Investigator traces to 1990s self-help titles and which Wikiquote prints in the Disputed section of its Thoreau page, citing Dan Millman’s The Life You Were Born to Live (1995), p. xi.

source.rightsNote: Meditations in Wall Street was first published in 1940. United States copyright in a work of that era survives only if the term was renewed in its 28th year, and we have not confirmed the renewal record either way, so treat the book as in copyright. Quote the single sentence as a short attributed excerpt; do not reproduce the book’s aphorisms at length.

author.name: Henry Stanley Haskins
author.heading: The anonymous man behind the maxim
author.bio: Haskins was a Wall Street trader who published Meditations in Wall Street anonymously in 1940 — a slim collection of aphorisms that Albert Jay Nock introduced without naming its author. Quote Investigator describes him as a Wall Street trader with a checkered background, and reports that The New York Times identified him as the book’s author in 1947. The Walden Woods Project gives his life dates as 1875–1957. His best-known sentence has spent most of its life wearing other people’s names.

misattribution.heading: Four wrong names
misattribution.intro: This sentence has been credited to at least four names that did not write it — three authors and a publishing house. Quote Investigator’s dated chronology runs William Morrow (1974), Ralph Waldo Emerson (1980), Oliver Wendell Holmes (1989) and finally Henry David Thoreau (1990s); the rows below lead with the credit this page exists to correct.

items.why: Quote Investigator places Thoreau-credited versions in spiritual-guidance books of the 1990s — the latest of the false credits, and the furthest from the source. The Walden Woods Project ↗ lists it on its Thoreau Mis-Quotation Page and corrects it to Haskins, Meditations in Wall Street (1940), p. 131.

By 1980 a university president was crediting the line to Emerson, per Quote Investigator ↗, which notes the quotation expert Ralph Keyes found no evidence Emerson said or wrote these words. Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed ↗ on Emerson’s page.
Quote Investigator records the 1989 bestseller The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People crediting the line to Oliver Wendell Holmes — one more name with no supporting text ↗.

items.scope: A publisher mistaken for an author
items.why: Because the book carried no author’s name, the imprint got read as one: Quote Investigator cites a Forbes item of 15 February 1974 crediting William Morrow, the publishing house ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence belongs to Henry Stanley Haskins, on page 131 of Meditations in Wall Street (William Morrow & Company, 1940) — a book he published anonymously, which is exactly why four better-known names ended up wearing his line. See the full chronology ↗.

context.heading: A stockbroker’s maxim in a transcendentalist’s coat
lead: It is quoted constantly, and almost never with the right name attached. The line was written for a 1940 book of Wall Street aphorisms, not in a nineteenth-century cabin: Meditations in Wall Street, published by William Morrow & Company with an introduction by Albert Jay Nock and no author’s name on the title page. Quote Investigator ↗ found the sentence on page 131 of that book, and reports that The New York Times named the trader Henry Stanley Haskins as the anonymous author in 1947.

That anonymity is the whole story. A maxim with no author attached is a vacancy, and famous names rush in to fill it. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the sentence drifting from an unnamed writer, to the publisher’s name in a 1974 Forbes item, to Ralph Waldo Emerson by 1980, to Oliver Wendell Holmes in a 1989 bestseller, and finally to Henry David Thoreau in spiritual-guidance books of the 1990s — each move making the line sound older and more authoritative than it is.
detailsBody: Thoreau is the last stop on a chain of upgrades, not the first. Quote Investigator places the Emerson credit in 1980 and the Thoreau versions in the 1990s, by which point the sentence had already been floating unattributed for decades. Thoreau and Emerson were friends and fellow transcendentalists, and both wrote a great deal about inwardness, so a stray aphorism about “what lies within us” slots into either name without friction.

The Walden Woods Project’s Thoreau Mis-Quotation Page ↗ exists precisely for this pattern, and lists the sentence with the correction to Haskins, Meditations in Wall Street (1940), p. 131. Wikiquote’s Thoreau page ↗ files the sentence under Disputed rather than Sourced: its earliest Thoreau citation is Dan Millman’s The Life You Were Born to Live (1995), p. xi, and it records that no occurrence has been located before the 1990s. There is no Thoreau text for it to be a variant of.
context.pull: An anonymous maxim is a vacancy. Famous names rush in to fill it.
